one_liner: Intel's own x86/x86-64 decoder and encoder in C; decodes faster than full-mode Zydis, roughly ties or trails Capstone once formatting is included.
what_it_does: A C library that turns 1-15 instruction bytes plus a machine mode into a xed_decoded_inst_t describing iclass, iform, ISA set, operands, implicit resources and flags, and formats it as Intel, AT&T or a detailed internal syntax via xed_format_context(). It also ships a generic encoder, a much faster function-per-instruction encoder (enc2), an instruction-length-only decoder (ILD) and a command-line tool. It is not a drop-in replacement for Capstone: the API, data structures and output strings are different.
how_it_is_fast: Decoder tables and enumerations are generated at build time by Python generators from text datafiles that describe an internal grammar of nonterminals, so decoding is a table-driven pipeline: an instruction length decode (ILD) pass, a static lookup of the xed_inst_t template, then generated nonterminal functions that capture operands. All decode state lives in the caller's xed_decoded_inst_t, with no allocation per instruction. Its strength is completeness and detail rather than raw speed; in both disas-bench runs the leaner decoders (iced, yaxpeax, diStorm) are several times faster.
when_to_use: You need the most complete and earliest coverage of new Intel ISA extensions: releases in 2025-2026 track APX, AVX10.2, AMX and ACE specification revisions and new chip configurations (Diamond Rapids, Nova Lake).

You need detailed per-operand semantics (read/write actions, implicit and suppressed operands, flags, ISA set and CPUID-based chip checks) for binary analysis, instrumentation or emulation, not just a text disassembly.
You need both a decoder and an encoder from one library, including the enc2 fast encoder for JIT-style code generation.
You only need instruction lengths: the ILD API (examples/xed-dec-ild.c, ILD-only builds) skips full operand decoding.
Your project is C or C++ and can accept Apache-2.0 and a static libxed.a.
when_not_to_use: Raw decode or disassembly throughput is the goal: iced decodes about 4.6x and diStorm about 1.7x faster in the 2021 run, and in the 2025 runs bddisasm and Zydis (min) also decode faster than XED.
You want to replace Capstone for decode+format speed: the 2025 runs on Ryzen 9 9950X and i9-13900K put XED at about 0.77x of Capstone.
You need non-x86 architectures (Capstone covers ARM, RISC-V and others).
Your build cannot run Python: libxed is produced by the mbuild Python build system (python 3.9 or later per docsrc/xed-build.txt), not CMake or a plain Makefile.
You need decoding that matches other disassemblers by default on recent XED: since v2025.03.02 LZCNT, TZCNT and PAUSE are off unless enabled, so F3 0F BD decodes as BSR.

integration.form: static lib (shared with --shared; installable kit with headers via 'mfile.py install')
integration.dependencies: build: Python 3.9+ and the separate intelxed/mbuild repository; runtime: only a few libc functions (memcmp, memset, memcpy, strcmp, strncat, strlen, fprintf, abort)
integration.min_toolchain: C compiler: GCC, Clang (Clang 17-20 named in 2025-2026 release notes) or MSVC; Python 3.9+ for the build
integration.platforms: Linux, Windows (with or without cygwin), FreeBSD per the docs; decodes IA-32 and Intel 64 code only; an open issue (#358) carries a macOS build fix
integration.thread_safety: Reentrant after a single xed_tables_init() call made before threads start; all decode/encode state lives in caller-provided structures.

gotchas: Call xed_tables_init() once before use, and re-initialise the decoded-instruction struct before every decode (xed_decoded_inst_zero_keep_mode() or xed_decoded_inst_zero_set_mode()); the benchmarks use xed_decoded_inst_zero plus set_mode each time.

Since v2025.03.02, PAUSE, LZCNT and TZCNT are disabled by default unless enabled through the decoder mode/chip-feature APIs (xed_set_decoder_modes, xed_chip_features_t), and unsupported PREFETCH decodes as NOP; default output therefore differs from other disassemblers on modern binaries.

No benchmark measures current XED: the 2021 icedland run used a decoder-only (--no-encoder) LTO build, the 2025 athre0z run used v2025.06.08 (submodule dc6bdbe) at --opt=3 without LTO, and v2026.02.17 later added systematic API input validation (disable with --no-api-check) whose cost is unmeasured.

Harness detail: the 2021 icedland bench/xed/main.c ignores xed_decode's error return and still calls xed_format_context and advances by the reported length on invalid bytes; the 2025 upstream version skips one byte per bad instruction and counts them. Each library is timed with clock() in one subprocess run, MB/s computed as MiB, so small gaps (XED 15.67 vs Capstone 14.02 MB/s) are within run-to-run noise.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick XED over iced, diStorm, yaxpeax-x86 or Zydis when Intel-authoritative ISA coverage, chip/ISA-set checks and an encoder matter more than speed; pick iced (Rust) or diStorm for the fastest decode, bddisasm or Zydis (min) for faster C decode with full operand info, and Zydis for faster decode+format with a permissive C API.
verified_claims_summary: In icedland/disas-bench (2021, i5-6600K, gcc 10.3.0, LTO builds, Firefox 86 xul.dll code section) XED decoded 55.39 MB/s against Zydis 34.19 and bddisasm 35.48 MB/s and did decode+format at 15.67 MB/s against Capstone's 14.02 MB/s; the upstream athre0z/disas-bench charts of October 2025 (Ryzen 9 9950X with GCC 13.3, i9-13900K with GCC 14.2, XED v2025.06.08 without LTO) show XED at about 0.77x of Capstone in decode+format and behind bddisasm and Zydis (min) in decode only, ahead only of full-mode Zydis.
status_note: Actively maintained by Intel (v2026.08.23, frequent ISA-alignment releases, 1.6k stars, 41 open issues including a few long-open decoder bugs such as #233 and #275); Apache-2.0 and copyable, but it is a mid-pack performer whose catalogue case rests on coverage rather than speed.
